extracted.intended_audience: graduate students or advanced undergraduates in algebraic topology; researchers learning about cohomology of fiber bundles and homotopy theory
extracted.subtask_description: Results, hypotheses, and examples for computing cohomology rings and module structures of fiber bundles (Leray–Hirsch, Gysin, Thom), minimal cell structures, and Hopf invariant properties in homotopy theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hopf invariant (definition and basic properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: When m = 2n−1 for a map f: S^{2n−1} → S^n the multiplicative structure of H^*(C_f) is determined by a relation α^2 = H(f) β for generators α ∈ H^n(C_f) and β ∈ H^{2n}(C_f), and the integer H(f) is the Hopf invariant of f. The sign depends on choice of generator β but can be fixed by identifying β with a fixed generator of H^{2n}(D^{2n}, ∂D^{2n}) via the characteristic map; composing f with a reflection of S^{2n−1} changes the sign of H(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: H(f) depends only on the homotopy class of f. If f is constant then H(f)=0 (C_f retracts onto S^n). For odd n, H(f)=0 because α^2 = −α^2 by graded commutativity, hence α^2 = 0. Examples: the Hopf attaching maps for CP^2, HP^2, OP^2 give H(f)=1 (with CP^2 and HP^2 explicitly noted). Maps arising from J_2(S^n) give H(f)=±2 when n is even. The Hopf invariant measures the multiplicative (cup-product) deviation from triviality in the mapping cone cohomology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adams theorem (Hopf invariant one) and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A map f: S^{2n−1} → S^n of Hopf invariant 1 exists only when n = 2, 4, 8 (Adams 1960).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rare existence has multiple topological consequences listed: R^n is a division algebra only for n = 1,2,4,8; S^n is an H–space only for n = 0,1,3,7; S^n has n linearly independent tangent vector fields only for n = 0,1,3,7; the only sphere fiber bundles S^p→S^q→S^r occur in the listed tuples (0,1,1), (1,3,2), (3,7,4), (7,15,8). Historical notes: earlier proofs of some consequences by Kervaire and Milnor, and Bott's theorem π_{2n}U(n) ≈ Z_{n!} are relevant. Use Adams' theorem as a strong obstruction: absence of Hopf-invariant-one maps rules out many algebraic/topological structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hopf invariant is a homomorphism (Proposition 4B.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hopf invariant H: π_{2n−1}(S^n) → Z is a homomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: compare mapping cones C_{f+g} and C_{f ∨ g} and analyze cohomology classes dual to the 2n-cells; induced maps send the relevant β classes so that α^2 for the wedge corresponds to H(f)β_f + H(g)β_g, yielding H(f+g) = H(f)+H(g). Corollary: when n is even, H or H/2 is a surjective homomorphism π_{2n−1}(S^n) → Z, so π_{2n−1}(S^n) contains a Z direct summand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal cell structure existence (Proposition 4C.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a simply-connected CW complex X and a decomposition of each H_n(X) as a direct sum of cyclic groups with specified generators, there exists a CW complex Z and a cellular homotopy equivalence f: Z → X such that each cell of Z is either (a) a 'generator' n-cell e^n_α mapping to the specified generator α of a cyclic summand of H_n(X), or (b) a 'relator' (n+1)-cell e^{n+1}_α whose cellular boundary equals a multiple of the corresponding generator n-cell when α has finite order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction given inductively on skeleta using the mapping cylinder and explicit choices of cycles and relators via the Hurewicz isomorphism. Caveat: the nonsimply-connected case can fail (examples: acyclic spaces, certain constructions with S^1 ∨ S^n ∪ e^{n+1}). The proposition gives a canonical 'minimal' CW model consistent with prescribed homology generators and torsion data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homotopy type determined by homology in adjacent dimensions (Example/Proposition 4C.2 & 4C.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a simply-connected CW complex X has only nonzero reduced homology groups H_n(X) (finitely generated) and H_{n+1}(X) (finitely generated free), then X is homotopy equivalent to a complex obtained from a wedge of n-spheres by attaching (n+1)-cells; attaching maps are determined up to homotopy by the cellular boundary map. In the special case that only H_2(X) ≈ Z_m and H_4(X) ≈ Z are nontrivial, the homotopy type of X is uniquely determined by the cup product ring H^*(X; Z) (applies to simply-connected closed 4-manifolds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The attaching maps are either trivial (generator (n+1)-cells) or represent multiples of inclusions (relator cells). For the 4-dimensional case, the cup product is represented by an m×m symmetric matrix (b_{jk}) with b_{jk}=a_{jk} and b_{jj}=a_j determined by the decomposition of the attaching map ϕ in terms of Hopf maps and Whitehead products; equality of cup-product matrices implies homotopy equivalence. Use these criteria to classify low-dimensional simply-connected complexes by (co)homology plus cup-product data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leray–Hirsch Theorem (Theorem 4D.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let F → E —p→ B be a fiber bundle and R a commutative coefficient ring. If (a) H^n(F; R) is a finitely generated free R-module for each n, and (b) there exist classes c_j ∈ H^{k_j}(E; R) whose restrictions i^*(c_j) form a basis for H^*(F; R) in each fiber (i: F → E inclusion), then the map H^*(B; R) ⊗_R H^*(F; R) → H^*(E; R) given by ∑ b_i ⊗ i^*(c_j) ↦ ∑ p^*(b_i) ∪ c_j is an isomorphism of R-modules. Equivalently, H^*(E; R) is a free H^*(B; R)-module with basis {c_j}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The conclusion is about module/additive structure, not generally a ring isomorphism (counterexample: Klein bottle as S^1-bundle over S^1 or Hopf bundle S^1→S^3→S^2). Proof by induction on the base CW-dimension using excision and relative arguments; key technical lemma: if (B,A) is k-connected then (E, p^{-1}(A)) is also k-connected. Typical applications: computing H^*(U(n)), H^*(Sp(n)), H^*(SU(n)), Grassmannians, flag manifolds; useful to obtain additive bases and to identify when cohomology of total space 'looks like' product cohomology. Check hypotheses carefully: freeness of H^*(F;R) and existence of global classes restricting fiberwise to a basis are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connectivity lifting lemma for bundles (Lemma 4D.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If p: E → B is a fiber bundle and A ⊂ B such that the pair (B, A) is k-connected, then the pair (E, p^{-1}(A)) is also k-connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via homotopy lifting property: homotopies in base lifting to homotopies in total space. Use this lemma in inductive proofs (e.g., in Leray–Hirsch) to pass connectivity properties from base to total space and reduce to skeleton arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative Leray–Hirsch (Theorem 4D.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a fiber bundle pair (F, F') → (E, E') —p→ B, if H^*(F, F'; R) is a free R-module, finitely generated in each dimension, and there exist classes c_j ∈ H^*(E, E'; R) whose restrictions form a basis for H^*(F, F'; R) in each fiber, then H^*(E, E'; R) is a free H^*(B; R)-module with basis {c_j}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The module structure uses the relative cup product H^*(E; R) × H^*(E, E'; R) → H^*(E, E'; R). Proof reduces the relative case to the absolute Leray–Hirsch by attaching mapping cylinders and using excision; useful precursor to the Thom isomorphism for disk bundles and to deriving the Gysin sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thom class and Thom isomorphism (definition and role)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a disk-bundle pair (D^n, S^{n−1}) → (E, E'), an element c ∈ H^n(E, E'; R) whose restriction to each fiber (D^n, S^{n−1}) is a generator of H^n(D^n, S^{n−1}; R) ≈ R is called a Thom class for the bundle. (R typically Z or Z_2.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Thom class yields the Thom isomorphism H^*(B; R) ≅ H^{*+n}(E, E'; R) for orientable disk bundles; the text sketches the route: deduce relative Leray–Hirsch, specialize to disk bundles, then show Thom isomorphism applies to orientable disk bundles. The Thom class is the cohomological datum encoding orientability and is central to deriving the Gysin sequence and computing Euler classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gysin sequence (for orientable sphere bundles)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an orientable sphere bundle S^{n−1} → E —p→ B (orientability holds if B is simply-connected or with Z_2 coefficients), there is a long exact Gysin sequence ... → H^{i−n}(B; R) —∪ e→ H^i(B; R) —p^*→ H^i(E; R) → H^{i−n+1}(B; R) → ... where e ∈ H^n(B; R) is the Euler class of the associated disk bundle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: for i < n−1, p^*: H^i(B) → H^i(E) is an isomorphism; if the bundle has a section then Euler class e = 0 and the Gysin sequence splits into short exact sequences, giving product-like cohomology (Künneth-type). The Euler class is an obstruction to a section: e ≠ 0 implies no section. Example applications: deriving that H^*(B; R) is polynomial Z[e] when the total space E is contractible (projective spaces), computing cohomology of unit tangent bundles and Grassmannians, and analyzing when splitting occurs (existence of vector fields). The Gysin sequence is derived by plugging the Thom isomorphism into the long exact sequence of the pair (disk bundle, sphere bundle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler class as obstruction to sections
rubrics_metrics.description: In a sphere bundle S^{n−1} → E —p→ B, the Euler class e ∈ H^n(B; R) satisfies: if the bundle has a section then e = 0; if e ≠ 0 then no section exists. In particular, e appears in the Gysin sequence as the map ∪ e: H^i(B) → H^{i+n}(B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Euler class of the unit tangent bundle of a closed orientable n-manifold M equals χ(M) times a generator of H^n(M; Z). Use Euler class computations to detect nonexistence of nowhere-vanishing vector fields (unit tangent vector field) and to determine splitting of Gysin sequence. For bundles with contractible total space, e generates polynomial cohomology of the base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of cohomology rings via Leray–Hirsch (Corollary 4D.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using Leray–Hirsch on the standard cell bundles yields cohomology ring descriptions: (a) H^*(U(n); Z) ≈ Λ_Z[x_1, x_3, ..., x_{2n−1}] (exterior algebra on generators in odd dimensions), (b) H^*(SU(n); Z) ≈ Λ_Z[x_3, x_5, ..., x_{2n−1}], (c) H^*(Sp(n); Z) ≈ Λ_Z[x_1, x_3, ..., x_{2n−1}] with appropriate degree shifts noted in text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction using bundles U(n−1)→U(n)→S^{2n−1}, Sp(n−1)→Sp(n)→S^{4n−1}, SU(n−1)→SU(n)→S^{2n−1} and applying Leray–Hirsch to get additive bases; graded-commutativity forces exterior algebra structure. Observe the ring isomorphism follows because cup products of distinct odd-degree generators are nonzero and powers vanish by degree reasons. Check base cases (U(1)=S^1, SU(2)=S^3) when inducting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology of Grassmannians as polynomial rings (Theorem 4D.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the complex Grassmannian G_n(C^∞), H^*(G_n(C^∞); Z) is a polynomial ring Z[c_1, ..., c_n] with c_i in degree 2i. Similarly, H^*(G_n(R^∞); Z_2) ≈ Z_2[w_1, ..., w_n] with w_i in degree i, and H^*(G_n(H^∞); Z) ≈ Z[q_1, ..., q_n] with q_i in degree 4i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: consider flag manifold F_n(C^∞) with cohomology Z[x_1, ..., x_n], apply Leray–Hirsch to the bundle F_n(C^∞) → G_n(C^∞) and show the pullback p^* is injective with image the symmetric polynomials in the x_i. Use classical algebra that symmetric polynomials form Z[σ_1, ..., σ_n] (σ_i degree i), compare Poincaré series to conclude surjectivity. Analogous arguments apply in real/quaternionic cases (use Z_2 coefficients in real case and rank/dimension counting). Useful criterion: compute Poincaré series to match ranks in each degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Gysin sequence to compute cup products and detect realizability (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples show how the Gysin sequence yields cup-product structures and realizability obstructions: e.g., for bundles with contractible total space and fiber S^{n−1}, Gysin implies H^*(B; Z) ≈ Z[e] (polynomial) for n>1 (use Z_2 for n=1); this forces n = 1,2,4 for existence of such bundles (projective-space bundles). Other examples: Grassmannians' universal bundles where Euler classes correspond to Stiefel-Whitney or Chern classes and quotienting by (e) yields cohomology of related classifying spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret the Gysin sequence concretely: when E contractible, ∪ e gives isomorphisms in cohomology shifting degrees by n; use that polynomial rings Z[e] appear only in certain degrees (2 or 4), giving strong existence constraints. In examples with covering spaces or determinant fibrations, analyze the portion of the Gysin sequence near low degrees to identify Euler classes and deduce quotient descriptions of cohomology rings (e.g., quotient by c_1).
